findings.title: Entry date: the default is 00:00 UTC and the test uses the bar's opening time, so the entry day is dropped on charts set to an American time zone (both scripts)
findings.what_goes_wrong: With the chart's time zone set to New York, to 'Exchange' on a US stock, or to any zone west of UTC, the Entry date field opens showing 2026-01-01 19:00 (18:00 in Mexico City, 21:00 in Buenos Aires). A user who changes only the date to the day of the buy gets 19:00 of that day, which is after that day's daily bar opened, so `time >= i_entryTime` is false for the entry day. On the entry day the Risk Desk table shows the warning 'Setup: type in the entry, a stop below it and the date', no bars are shaded and the stop alert is not armed; from the next day on the count is one short ('day 1' on day 2) and the time-up alert comes a day late. Typing the fill time (for example 10:15) drops the entry day in every time zone, because a daily bar's `time` is its opening time. On a weekly or monthly chart `time` is the first session's open, so the position is not recognised for the rest of the entry week or month. With the chart on UTC or a European zone and the time left untouched, the current code happens to work.

answers.answer: Not documented, so not established. By analogy with syminfo.* the value should be the requested symbol's, but no TradingView page says so for earnings.future_*, and the compiler cannot tell. It can be settled in one look: on a SPY daily chart (SPY's own value is na) a number in Portfolio Desk's Earnings column proves the requested symbol's date is returned. User Manual, Other timeframes and data, read 12 Nov 2026: "Scripts can also retrieve information about upcoming earnings and dividends for an instrument via the earnings.future_* and dividends.future_* built-in variables." answers.answer: No error. An empty symbol string requests the chart's own symbol, and input.symbol("") is the documented way to default to it. ignore_invalid_symbol = true changes nothing for ""; it only turns a symbol that cannot be resolved into na instead of a runtime error. Two consequences: a row with shares above 0 and no symbol becomes a position in the chart's symbol (the script names it correctly), and a symbol without data silently drops out of the book (finding 'NO DATA'). Once a symbol has been picked the field cannot be emptied again except with 'Reset settings', so 'shares = 0 switches the row off' is the right design.
answers.evidence: User Manual, Other timeframes and data (read 12 Nov 2026): "Users can also pass an empty string to this parameter, which prompts the function to use the current chart's symbol." Inputs page, Symbol input: `string symbolInput = input.symbol("", "Symbol")`, "The defval argument in the input.symbol() call is an empty "string".", "By default, it is an empty "string", which specifies the main symbol." pine_requests.md section 4.1: ignore_invalid_symbol "true returns na instead of a runtime error".

answers.answer: Intraday (line 140, f_prev with lookahead_on): historical bars that belong to daily bar D, and the realtime bar, both use day D-1. Same on history and in realtime, no repaint, no look-ahead. But after D has closed (evening, post-market, next pre-market) it is still D-1, one day older than the label 'last completed day' (finding). The day count is also one short there (finding). Daily chart: the chart's own bars (line 139); a historical bar has its final values, the realtime bar moves until its close; the two requests are computed and not used. The index on a daily chart is a same-timeframe request of another symbol without offset: same-day values, documented as free of repainting. Above 1D (line 141, a lower-timeframe request with lookahead_off): historical bars use the last daily bar inside the week or month, the realtime bar uses the latest daily bar; equal to the daily chart, no look-ahead. What is wrong above 1D is the use of the chart bar's own time and time_close for the position and for earnings (two findings). Requesting "1D" on a 1D chart with lookahead_on is harmless: documented as an accepted case, and its results are not used on that timeframe.

answers.answer: Signature and use are correct: ticker.modify(tickerid, session, adjustment, backadjustment, settlement_as_close), with session.regular as second argument. It keeps the chart's other modifiers (adjustment) and forces the regular session, so the daily values do not change when extended hours are switched on. For symbols without sessions the modifier is ignored. With extended hours on an intraday chart: the price used for the plan and the low used for the stop alert include pre- and post-market prints, and during those hours the daily values are a further day old (same finding as in Q3). The daily-chart path reads the chart's own bars, not symD; the documentation says end-of-day feeds carry no extended-hours data, so the two should agree, but that was not checked on a chart.

answers.answer: Yes: realtime only, once per closed bar. Several alert() calls executed at the same close each send their own message, so none is swallowed. The transition logic of Portfolio Desk is correct: before every realtime tick the var arrays and wasHot are rolled back to the state committed at the previous bar's close, so writing them on every tick is harmless and each comparison is against the previous closed bar. The first realtime bar cannot send a spurious message: the state is built on every historical bar, alert() does nothing there, and when the market is closed the last bar is a historical one. Two things that are not spurious but worth knowing: the stop message is level-triggered and repeats every bar (finding), and at the chart symbol's closing tick the other symbols' values are whatever had arrived, which the docs describe as a possible race.
answers.evidence: Alerts page (https://www.tradingview.com/pine-script-docs/concepts/alerts/, read 12 Nov 2026): "Alerts only trigger in the realtime bar."; alert.freq_once_per_bar_close: "An alert is only triggered when the realtime bar closes and an alert() call is executed during that script iteration."; the example alert "will only trigger the first time each of the alert() calls is executed during the realtime bar." Execution model (https://www.tradingview.com/pine-script-docs/language/execution-model/): "Rollback reverts all variables declared with var before the current bar to the last committed states"; for objects referenced by var variables "the rollback process reverts any changes to those objects that occur on the open bar"; "The system commits the script's data for the realtime bar only after the bar closes." pine_requests.md section 4.3 for the race.

answers.answer: The variable holds one value, today's next report, on every bar. On historical bars 'sessions to earnings' is therefore a countdown to today's next date and means nothing as history (the 'Sessions to earnings' series in a CSV export should be read on the last bar only). In an alert the date is frozen at creation: the alert covers that one report, does not see a date that is moved afterwards, and knows nothing once it has passed. answers.answer: The book mathematics is the calibration's. WU_i = shares x ATR x sqrt(h) / equity is w_i x u_i; varP = sum WU_i^2 + 2 sum_{i<j} WU_i rho_ij WU_j is the einsum of g70; the band is s_p x quantile as a fraction of equity, and g70's outcome is the simple return sum(w x (c[t+h]/c[t] - 1)), also a fraction of equity; correlations are of log returns in both. f_corr divides covariance and variances by the same n, so it equals np.corrcoef. On the last bar RM holds one row per chart bar for the last 60 chart bars including the current one (the var matrix is rolled back on each realtime tick, so the developing bar is one row), which is g70's ret[t-59..t] when every position shares the chart's calendar. It is not that when calendars differ (finding on line 141). "Independent positions" = (sum WU)^2 / varP is 1 for perfectly correlated positions and N for independent equal ones; correct, but its warning threshold is always met (finding on line 333). Open risk = sum of shares x max(close - stop, 0) / equity, from the last close, as the input tooltip says; the At-risk column tooltip says otherwise (finding on line 304). Edge cases: stop above entry -> CHECK ENTRY / STOP, R "-", "NaN R" in alerts; stop 0 -> row says "no stop" but book open risk counts 0 for it; entry 0 -> R "-", status CHECK, result excluded, as intended; entered today -> not counted as day 1 when the chart time zone is west of UTC or a fill time is typed (finding on risk desk line 36, same code at portfolio line 115); fewer than 60 bars -> correlation on the common days if at least 20, else 0.3, and with fewer than 14 bars the position disappears from the table and the totals; same symbol in two slots -> correlation 1, s_p and nEff treat them as one position, the average correlation includes that 1; non-US symbol on a US chart -> repeated and dropped returns, day count is in the symbol's own bars (correct), currency not converted.

answers.answer: Plan arithmetic is what the labels say: stop distance = k x daily ATR, shares = floor(min(risk cash / distance, cap / price)), value, % of equity, money at risk = shares x distance. verdicts.title: Entry date: the default is 00:00 UTC and the test uses the bar's opening time, so the entry day is dropped on charts set to an American time zone (both scripts)
verdicts.reason: Could not refute. The default is midnight UTC, the widget shows and reads it in the chart's time zone, and the test compares it with the bar's OPENING time. On a chart set to New York, Exchange (US stock) or any zone west of UTC the field shows 19:00 of the previous day; changing only the date gives 19:00 of the entry day, which is after that day's daily bar opened (09:30). Result by the code: posOn is false on the entry day (table shows the 'Setup' warning, no shading, stop alert not armed), held starts one day late, time-up one day late; Portfolio Desk shows '-' in Day and cannot report a stop touch that day (line 233 needs HLD >= 1). Typing a fill time after the open drops the entry day in every zone. With UTC or a zone east of UTC and the time untouched it works, as the reviewer says. The proposed fix is sound for stocks, 24-hour symbols and forex (checked by hand) and compiles. One assumption is not documented and not verified on a chart: that a daily bar's time_close is that day's session close (16:00 New York), not the next session's open. If it were the next open, the day before the entry would be counted.
verdicts.evidence: Read 12 Nov 2026. Inputs page (https://www.tradingview.com/pine-script-docs/concepts/inputs/): input.time() "converts a user-specified date and time, in the chart's time zone, into a time zone-agnostic UNIX timestamp"; "Changing the time zone in the chart's settings can change the values shown in the input fields." Time page (https://www.tradingview.com/pine-script-docs/concepts/time/): "The time variable holds the UNIX timestamp of the current bar's opening time"; "Unlike the other two signatures, the default time zone for the third signature is GMT+0."; "If the dateString argument does not specify the time of day, the timestamp() call considers the time 00:00 (midnight)." verdicts.title: Lines and labels anchored up to 400 bars back are drawn on realtime bars without reserving the `time` buffer
verdicts.reason: The code matches the failing example in TradingView's own error page almost line for line. When the market is open at load, on a 24-hour symbol, and in the server-side alert instance, barstate.islast is first true on a realtime bar, so the first request for `time` that far back happens where buffers are no longer resized. When the market is closed at load the reference happens on the last historical bar and the buffer is grown there, but the offset then grows by one with every new bar (until the 400 cap) and can pass the size that was set. The size of the default `time` buffer is not published (only 'fewer than 500'), so the exact offset at which it fails is unknown; that is the only unverified part. Note that even plan mode draws 4 bars back on realtime bars; the fix covers that too. The fix is the one the error page prescribes, it is cheap (one series, 500 values) and it compiles.

verdicts.title: `eInside[1]` and `timeUp[1]` are first evaluated on a realtime bar, on the bar where their alert should fire
verdicts.reason: Neither shown nor refuted. The premise is right: `and` is lazy in v6, so in lines 211, 214 and 226 the `[1]` is read only when the left side is true, which for a fresh alert first happens on a realtime bar. Whether that read can fail depends on how the buffer of a variable is sized when its only history reference is a literal offset that never executes on historical bars, and no page I read says. Pointing towards 'no defect': the error page says constant offsets work without issues; its failing examples all use offsets that change between historical and realtime bars or offsets passed through a function; the compiler warns about function calls inside lazy expressions but gives no warning for `x[1]` on a global variable (probe); and `if cond and not cond[1]` is an everyday pattern. Pointing the other way: the v5 error page says detection fails when the flow of execution does not let Pine inspect a series used inside a conditional branch. Applying the fix is harmless: the four previous-bar values are read at global scope on every bar, the values are identical (they are global variables), and the cost is nil. I would apply it.
